watch_next: October 8 in-depth discussion of the special town meeting warrant articles
November 17 special town meeting

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee expects to fund an outside review of the school department's FY26 budget variance from its own reserve account.

Draft special town meeting articles got a first look -- stormwater fees, a veterans' exemption increase, PAC salaries, a track/turf field engineering request, and a special education reserve transfer.
Those articles move to an in-depth discussion October 8 and a public hearing October 22, ahead of a November 17 special town meeting.
A workshop on net school spending was tabled because the presenter could not attend.
Whether to hold joint tri-board meetings, on topics including an athletics budget and ambulance billing write-offs, was left to the three board chairs to work out.

why_it_matters: The planned review would look at why the school department's FY26 spending diverged from its budget, a question tied to special education placement costs.
The special education reserve transfer, the track/turf field funding, and a possible veterans' exemption increase would all go to voters at the November 17 special town meeting.
A new stormwater fee structure, discussed at this meeting, could show up as a separate charge on future bills depending on how the article is written.

ours.headline: FinCom will likely fund an outside review of the school department's FY26 budget overruns from its reserve

watch_next: Select Board and School Committee action on the RAP fund and school choice offset for article three, expected the week following this meeting
The special town meeting vote on all three warrant articles

what_happened.line: Finance Committee unanimously recommended the school spending plan funded by new state aid, covering a second grade teacher, reading specialist, assistant principal, music teacher, and reduced athletic transportation costs.
The committee deferred the second warrant article to town meeting itself, since its own petitioner plans to move to pass it over.

The committee also deferred the third article, covering middle and high school sports funding, because its funding source had not yet been established by the Select Board or ratified by the School Committee.

Town officials informally agreed to apply a school choice credit to reduce the amount needed for the sports-funding article, pending action by the Select Board and School Committee the following week.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote on all three warrant articles at the special town meeting, including whether to fund the school positions and restored athletic transportation described in article one.

The mechanism behind article three -- a possible new special-purpose fund drawn from RAP money -- was still undecided at this meeting, so what residents vote on for sports funding may change before town meeting.

Town counsel advised that the article three motion will be worded more generally than the printed warrant article, since town meeting cannot legally earmark school-budget funds for a specific purpose.

ours.headline: Finance Committee recommended the new-state-aid school spending plan, but deferred the funding source for the rest of the warrant to town meeting itself.

watch_next: Select board meeting, August 18, on where WRAP snow-and-ice funds are directed
Finance Committee public hearing on the citizens petition, August 27

what_happened.line: A resident presented a cost model for a citizens petition to restore cut school sports and transportation ahead of the August 27 public hearing.
The chair asked the school committee to meet before that hearing, and the petitioner was directed to work out the funding mechanism with the town manager, select board, and town counsel.

Town counsel's opinion on what counts as "other available funds" for the article will be circulated, and the select board will decide August 18 whether new state snow-and-ice reimbursement money goes into a restricted fund or free cash.
The committee concluded the Finance Committee Reserve Fund likely cannot be used for the petition article, since the need appears foreseeable rather than an emergency.
The superintendent proposed directing any additional state aid toward literacy staffing and behavioral support rather than general class-size reduction, which drew extended debate.

why_it_matters: Town meeting will be asked to vote on the citizens petition article, and how it would be funded is not yet resolved.
Whether free cash, a state reimbursement fund, or the Reserve Fund can legally cover the article affects whether the article as written can proceed or needs to be scaled back on the floor.
How the district would spend any additional state aid -- staffing versus class size -- is now part of the same funding conversation.

ours.headline: The town is racing to fund a citizens petition restoring cut sports and transportation before the August 27 hearing.

watch_next: August 13 special town meeting presentation from the school committee, superintendent and petitioner Mandy Gilman
August 27 public hearing on the warrant article

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee heard the superintendent's plan to use FY27 state aid gains plus health insurance savings to fund five items, including two reading specialists, a full-time vice principal and tutoring seats.

An additional special town meeting is expected before September 3; a joint presentation from the school committee, superintendent and petitioner Mandy Gilman is set for August 13, with a public hearing on the article August 27.
The committee reorganized for the year, re-electing Chris Manard as chair and electing Peter Beardmore vice chair and Tom Gray clerk.
Department and school budget preview presentations, previously done jointly with the tri-board, will move to November or December, ahead of formal budget season.
The committee's capital planning committee seat was left unfilled and tabled for a future meeting.

why_it_matters: The staffing items the superintendent wants funded -- reading specialists, tutoring seats, a full-time vice principal and music teacher -- touch classrooms directly and are proposed to be paid from state aid and health insurance savings rather than new local tax dollars.
The special town meeting warrant article gets a public airing August 13 and a formal hearing August 27, which is where residents can weigh in before any vote.
Moving budget preview presentations earlier, to November/December, changes when residents can first see department and school budget details each cycle.

ours.headline: Finance Committee reorganized under new leadership and moved budget previews earlier ahead of a special town meeting

watch_next: A future Finance Committee meeting where year-end transfers and the fiscal policy list are actually taken up
Whether the chair, once back, moves the July reorg/vice-chair election date

what_happened.line: With the chair away, Finance Committee deferred year-end transfers to a future meeting rather than acting on them.
The committee compiled a list of fiscal policies to review later, including free cash, revenue projections, stabilization accounts and OPEB, without voting on any.
Members discussed reviving a joint committee with the Select Board and School Committee but reached no consensus, leaving it for the chair to take up on his return.
Election of a new vice chair was postponed until the chair is back, with the usual July date now in question for one member's availability.

why_it_matters: Year-end transfers move town money between budget lines after the fact, and residents will not see that reconciliation until a later meeting.
The stabilization-account policy under discussion touches when reserves such as the fire truck fund can be tapped versus held for one-time needs.
A revived tri-board committee would change how the Select Board, School Committee and Finance Committee coordinate on shared fiscal decisions.

ours.headline: Finance Committee, minus its chair, deferred nearly every substantive item — transfers, policy review, tri-board revival — to a future meeting.

watch_next: Next Finance Committee meeting, June 11
Whether the state Senate aid to Lunenburg is finalized and signed into law

what_happened.line: Finance Committee weighed reopening the FY27 school budget after new state Senate aid, but took no formal action, leaving the town-meeting-approved budget in place.
A member urged that any alternate budget proposal next year be vetted by the finance committee and tri-board before reaching town meeting.
Members debated revisiting reserve, free cash, and OPEB contribution policy given the tight budget year, without resolving the question.
The chair said any additional state aid, once finalized, would not be spent all at once and could instead be allocated at a special town meeting.
The committee set its next meeting for June 11th and agreed to resume work on the financial policies document ahead of FY28.

why_it_matters: Whether the FY27 school budget already approved at town meeting gets reopened affects how much of the new state aid reaches classrooms versus reserves.
A special town meeting could be called to allocate any finalized state aid, which would be a vote residents get to weigh in on.
Reserve, free cash, and OPEB funding levels shape how much cushion the town has for future budget years and how steep future tax asks could be.

ours.headline: Committee debated reopening FY27 school budget after new state Senate aid, but leaned toward not disturbing the town-meeting-approved budget

watch_next: May town meeting, where article L (FY27 budget) and article M (the two override tiers) go to a town-wide vote
Finance Committee meeting, April 23

what_happened.line: Finance Committee voted 4-2 to recommend both tiers of a Proposition 2½ override for town meeting.
The FY27 omnibus balanced budget was recommended on a split 4-1-1 vote after a member argued it under-documents two new positions.
The committee voted 4-2 to add the assistant town manager and HR director positions to the salary grid, which a member said bypassed the town's normal job-description process.
Several prior 5-0 and other warrant-article recommendations were re-voted so the chair's vote could be added before the warrant is finalized.
The next Finance Committee meeting was set for April 23, skipping April 9.

why_it_matters: Town meeting will vote on both override tiers as well as the underlying FY27 budget, so a resident's tax bill depends on which of these articles pass.
Adding the two new town-hall positions to the salary grid affects what those roles cost the town, and the committee's recommendation was split, not unanimous.
The re-votes and the finance committee's own annual report will accompany the warrant residents receive by mail before they vote.

ours.headline: Finance Committee voted to recommend both Prop 2½ override tiers for town meeting, 4-2 each

watch_next: The next Finance Committee meeting, when the full board is expected to take up the override recommendation.
A future vote on the FY27 omnibus town/school budget article, once closeout and transfer figures are final.

what_happened.line: The committee put off recommending a position on the FY27 Proposition 2½ override until the full five-member board can meet.
It also deferred the FY27 omnibus town and school operating budget because final transfer figures were not yet ready.
A new special-purpose health insurance stabilization fund transfer passed its recommendation on a 4-1 vote.
A proposed Assistant Town Manager/HR Director grade change was pushed to the next meeting after members said it needed further discussion.
Most routine warrant articles -- revolving funds, the FY27 capital budget, and the water and solid waste enterprise funds -- were recommended for approval.

why_it_matters: The override recommendation touches what residents are asked to approve at town meeting or the ballot, and the committee is not yet on record with a position.
The FY27 omnibus budget funds town and school operations for the coming year; its numbers were not final at this meeting.
The health insurance stabilization fund is a new savings mechanism for a cost that affects both town and school budgets, and it did not pass without dissent.

ours.headline: Finance Committee set warrant recommendations but held its override vote for the full board

watch_next: April 6 virtual Finance Committee meeting: vote on warrant articles and the committee's report
May 2 town meeting warrant vote and May 16 override ballot vote

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee closed its public hearing on the FY27 school and town budgets without voting on the budget, an override, or any warrant article.

The superintendent laid out a level-funded budget with cuts to teaching positions, music, and athletics, against two override scenarios that would restore and add staff across schools, police, fire, DPW, and the library.
Draft warrant articles, including the override article itself, were walked through but not voted on.
The committee scheduled an additional virtual meeting for April 6 to vote on the warrant articles and finalize its report before the town meeting deadline.

why_it_matters: Whether voters pass a tier-1 or tier-2 override in May decides whether class sizes rise and positions such as teachers, a custodian, and an occupational therapy assistant go unfilled.
The warrant articles still being drafted will set exactly what residents are asked to vote on at town meeting and on the override ballot.
Town departments including police, fire, DPW, and the library face the same level-funded-versus-override choice as the schools.

ours.headline: School and town budgets face deep cuts unless voters pass a tier-1 or tier-2 override in May

watch_next: Continued public hearing, March 26 at 7:00
School Committee's voted budget presentation to the Finance Committee

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee opened its budget public hearing and voted to continue it to March 26 at 7:00.
A member said town bylaw requires the School Committee to present the budget it actually voted, with an explanation of major changes, not just a single line item.
The committee said it has not yet received an updated budget snapshot from the Select Board's own budget workshop with the town manager.
Both the school and town sides are expected to bring a core-services budget and a separate restoration or override budget rather than one dollar figure.
A member said residents need to know what a 'no' vote on the override would actually cut, not just see a total.

why_it_matters: Residents will eventually be asked to vote on an override, and this hearing is where the town and school budgets that frame that choice get explained before town meeting.
The bylaw question about the School Committee presenting its full voted budget, not just a line item, affects how much detail the public sees before deciding.
A continued hearing means the public comment window on the budget stays open into late March rather than closing now.

ours.headline: Finance Committee opened its budget public hearing and immediately continued it to March 26.

watch_next: The rescheduled FY27 budget public hearing on March 26
The tri-board meeting on March 19 to resolve the one-override-vs-two-override question

what_happened.line: Finance Committee recapped a tri-board session where all members agreed an override belongs on the ballot, but remained split on whether it should be one amount or two.

DPW's proposed FY27 budget came in higher than prior years, restoring pavement management funding the town manager's preliminary budget had cut, though one committee member said they will not support that restoration.
The town manager's office is being restructured: the communications and IT director position would be eliminated and a new assistant town manager position funded starting July 1.

The committee recommended moving a warrant article seeking money to legally investigate several neglected municipal trust funds from the annual town meeting to a special town meeting, so a firmer cost estimate can be developed first.
The FY27 budget public hearing was pushed back one week to March 26, with a tri-board meeting taking the committee's March 19 slot instead.

why_it_matters: An override, once the ballot format is settled, would raise property taxes for residents and the one-question-versus-two split changes how they vote on it.
The DPW budget still has to be finalized, and whether pavement management funding is restored affects road paving work and how storm water permit compliance gets funded.
The town manager's office restructuring changes which staff position handles human resources and IT/communications duties going forward.

ours.headline: Finance Committee reviewed FY27 department budgets amid a large town-school funding gap, with an override now expected.

watch_next: Tri-board meeting on the FY27 budget and override, March 10, 7:30pm, Town Hall (or Zoom)
PAC's promised breakdown of staff time between government and public-channel programming

what_happened.line: Finance Committee members leaned toward asking voters for a trimmed, level-service Proposition 2½ override rather than bundling town requests with the school committee's larger 'restoration' budget.
The concern was explicit: a 2012 override bundled similarly and failed by roughly two-to-one, leading to a decade of cuts.
The override's shape now goes to a tri-board meeting of town and school officials on March 10.

Public Access Cable described a widening deficit from falling Comcast franchise fees and a forced studio move, and agreed to start tracking how its staff time splits between government and public-channel work.
The Council on Aging presented a level-funded budget and the Library a modest increase, with a member asking the library to itemize all funding sources next time.

why_it_matters: Whether the town bundles a school 'restoration' ask into one override question or asks for less, level-service money affects every taxpayer's ballot choice and, town officials warned, whether any of it passes at all.
Public Access Cable's declining franchise-fee revenue and relocation could affect coverage of town and school meetings if the town doesn't take up funding it.
The library's state certification and state aid depend on the town meeting a minimum appropriation threshold, which this budget cycle sets.

ours.headline: Finance Committee warns a large school 'restoration' override could fail, as one did in 2012.

watch_next: March 11 tri-board meeting on override structure (single-year vs. multi-year, use of excess levy capacity)
March 12 Finance Committee review of smaller department budgets (Council on Aging, Board of Health)

what_happened.line: The School Committee chair said a townwide operating override, not a smaller fix, is needed to avoid what he called "catastrophic" cuts.
The district's FY27 school budget presentation focused on restoring special education, literacy, and student-services positions cut the prior year.
No budget votes were taken; the schools will get a single line within the town's balanced budget, and the district must scale its ask down to that number if an override fails.
IT presented an FY27 request driven largely by the loss of one-time ARPA funding that had covered MUNIS software.
The business manager agreed to compile ongoing EPIMS staffing trend data for the Finance Committee and the tri-board.

why_it_matters: An operating override, if pursued, would go to voters and change property tax bills beyond the normal 2½ percent cap.
The positions under discussion -- special education, literacy, and student-services roles cut last year -- affect direct school services to students.
Override structure and size will be worked out at the March 11 tri-board meeting before going to the Select Board for a warrant.

ours.headline: School Committee says only a townwide override can restore positions cut last year, not a smaller fix.

watch_next: Annual Town Meeting, May 2, 2026
Finance Committee public budget hearing, currently slated for March 19 but flagged by members as possibly premature

what_happened.line: The Town Manager presented a preliminary FY27 town budget that does not balance and currently relies on a Proposition 2½ override.
No votes were taken on the budget or the override; the presentation was informational only.
The fire department outlined a fourth-shift staffing proposal as its main FY27 cost driver.
Police described shifting from two school resource officers to one SRO plus a second detective, citing cyber crimes against children.
FY25 books closed late, risking a hold on state aid; the town secured a filing extension.

why_it_matters: An override, if it reaches a ballot, would raise property taxes beyond the state cap and needs voter approval.
The fire department's added shift and the police restructuring both affect staffing levels and response for residents.
A late FY25 closeout touches the town's cash flow and its standing for state aid, even though an extension was obtained.

ours.headline: Town Manager unveiled a preliminary FY27 budget that does not balance without a property tax override

watch_next: Police, fire, and facilities budget presentations at next week's meeting
A specific FY27 override amount, not yet determined at this meeting

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee was told a level-service town and school budget is unlikely to balance without a Proposition 2½ override, with no amount yet set.
The town's health insurance increase came in lower than earlier feared after the insurance trust dropped coverage of a weight-loss drug class.
The committee agreed to formally ask the school department to present its FY27 budget in the same format as prior years, with staffing per line and one combined athletics budget.
The chair warned that even if an override passes this year, another level-service override could be needed again next year.
A member questioned why a turf field replacement is before the Capital Planning Committee despite never being a ranked school priority.

why_it_matters: A property tax override vote looks likely for residents this year, and the committee flagged it may not be the last one.
How the school budget gets presented -- staffing counts and a single athletics total -- shapes what residents can actually compare before any override vote.
Health insurance costs are one input into whether a level-service budget needs cuts, an override, or both.

ours.headline: FinCom previews FY27 budget: a level-service plan likely still needs an override, possibly again next year.

watch_next: School budget presentation to the Finance Committee, February 19
Warrant articles for the May 2 annual town meeting due March 16

what_happened.line: The town manager said an override or cuts are likely for FY27, citing budget pressure across departments.
Lunenburg's FY27 assessment to Monty Tech would rise mainly because of the state's minimum contribution formula, not Monty Tech's own spending growth.
A storm water task force proposed a dedicated utility funded by a flat homeowner fee; several committee members argued the operating budget would be more efficient.
The finance department reported ongoing staff turnover and FY25 books still not closed, complicating FY27 budget preparation.
A preliminary FY27 capital plan listing ranked projects across departments was presented, pending free cash certification.

why_it_matters: An override, if it goes to a town-wide vote, would raise property tax bills beyond the normal cap and residents would decide it directly.
A separate storm water utility, if adopted, would likely show up as a new fee on homeowners rather than as part of the existing tax-funded budget.
Monty Tech's assessment increase and Lunenburg's own department budgets both feed the same FY27 town budget that goes to the May 2 annual town meeting.

ours.headline: Monty Tech's FY27 assessment to Lunenburg would jump sharply, and the town manager warned an override is likely.

watch_next: The finalized FY27 revenue estimate once the town manager completes it
Department budgets submitted under the requested 5% reduction scenario, with narrative explanations

what_happened.line: A preliminary FY27 revenue estimate leaves little room for other cost increases once health insurance rises, intensifying override debate.
The finance office is described as being in crisis: the finance director has departed, FY25 remains unclosed, and a retired accountant is filling in part time.
A committee member urged cuts to recycling, the TCP building, ambulance receipts and capital funding before supporting any override.
The town manager warned that a budget built without an override would likely mean real staffing and service cuts.
Monty Tech and the schools will be brought into the budget calendar earlier, and department heads must submit a 5% reduction scenario.

why_it_matters: A possible Proposition 2½ override for FY27 would go to voters, and this meeting weighed what cuts to town services might come first.
Requiring departments to model a 5% reduction, and moving the school and Monty Tech budgets earlier in the calendar, could change which programs and staffing residents see proposed and when.
An unclosed FY25 and a vacant finance director post touch how reliable the town's current financial reporting is while these budget decisions are being made.

ours.headline: FinCom says FY27 leaves almost no room after health insurance; a school override looms and deep cuts are floated

watch_next: Nov. 18, 2025 special town meeting, where the deferred articles go to a vote
Next Finance Committee meeting, Dec. 11

what_happened.line: The committee deferred several contested or under-documented warrant articles -- a special education reserve fund, a stormwater consulting item, an expanded senior tax deferral, and two salary-plan changes -- to Town Meeting without a recommendation, pending more detail from the town manager.
Its vote on eliminating the volunteer Personnel Committee and shifting its authority to the town manager ended inconclusive, roughly one in favor, two opposed, one deferring.
The committee voted, 3-2, not to recommend replacing mailed warrant booklets with a postcard notice, a change pitched as a mailing-cost saving.
It approved, 3-1, a transfer to hire outside consultants for capital project cost estimating, after debate over how the funding moves between capital accounts.

why_it_matters: Residents at the Nov. 18 special town meeting will vote on the deferred articles -- special education reserve funding, senior tax deferral eligibility, and salary-plan changes -- without a Finance Committee recommendation attached.
Eliminating the Personnel Committee would move authority over town personnel and salary administration to the town manager, a governance change separate from any single budget line.
How town meeting warrants get distributed -- full booklet or mailed notice -- affects how residents learn what they're being asked to vote on.

ours.headline: Finance Committee splits on scrapping the Personnel Committee; defers most Nov. 18 warrant articles to Town Meeting

watch_next: Nov. 13 public hearing where the Finance Committee will make recommendations on all 17 warrant articles
A tri-board meeting on school budget, likely scheduled for Thanksgiving week

what_happened.line: Finance Committee reviewed all 17 special town meeting warrant articles but deferred recommendations to the Nov. 13 public hearing.
Two articles on the FY26 budget amendment and a prior-year hospital bill will go to town meeting without a committee recommendation.
New growth actuals are coming in above the budgeted estimate, prompting a raise-and-appropriate article; members disputed the exact figure.
PAC's fee revenue is running below its budget and retained-earnings draw, raising a sustainability question the tri-board will take up separately.
The tri-board will give the school budget its own dedicated meeting, likely during Thanksgiving week since Nov. 18 town meeting night will not work.

why_it_matters: Town meeting voters will decide the FY26 budget amendment, a prior-year bill, a special education reserve fund, and other transfers without a Finance Committee recommendation attached until Nov. 13.
A proposed 41A expansion and MBTA zoning compliance article are both on the warrant and could affect senior tax deferrals and local zoning rules.
PAC's budget shortfall and the personnel committee's proposed elimination are unresolved questions that residents may hear more about at the Nov. 13 hearing or a later tri-board meeting.

ours.headline: Finance Committee reviewed all 17 special town meeting warrant articles, deferring recommendations to the Nov. 13 public hearing

watch_next: October 23 Finance Committee meeting -- vote/hearing on the Special Town Meeting warrant
November 18 Special Town Meeting

what_happened.line: Finance Committee members said two warrant articles -- eliminating the Personnel Committee and merging the APDC into the Historical Commission -- are premature for the November Special Town Meeting and need more public process first.
The committee put off voting on the full Special Town Meeting warrant, setting its October 23 meeting as both the vote and the hearing required before the November 18 Special Town Meeting.
A member raised the school district's FY26 budget as a large increase over FY25 spending, noting the override and a further increase compounded across two years.
Members questioned paying for full architectural design work on the Ritter/Town Hall building project before getting a rough cost-per-square-foot estimate.
The committee agreed to ask tri-board presenters to send budget materials about a week ahead of meetings instead of the day of.

why_it_matters: The Personnel Committee and APDC articles would change who handles town personnel policy and architectural/historic review, and residents will be asked to vote on them at the November 18 Special Town Meeting.
The FY26 school budget comparison touches one of the largest lines in the town's spending plan, which factors into the tax bill.
How building costs like Ritter/Town Hall are estimated affects what capital spending taxpayers are eventually asked to approve.

ours.headline: Finance Committee pushed back on rushing Personnel Committee/APDC bylaw changes to November Town Meeting

watch_next: October 20: new finance director Katie McKenna starts
October 23: finance committee reviews the Q1 FY26 Munis report

what_happened.line: The town's entire finance department is turning over at once, with a new finance director due to start amid interim coverage.
The finance committee voted unanimously to send its completed master planning committee questionnaire responses to the steering committee.
The town manager recommended dropping a partial roof repair project from the town meeting warrant, routing it through the normal capital planning process instead.
The committee continued questioning a reported gap between school spending and the current fiscal year's budget baseline, without resolving it.
The committee set an October date to review the first-quarter Munis report and pushed a review of town finance policies to November.

why_it_matters: A full turnover in the finance office, including the director, payroll/benefits administrator and assistant accountant, touches how the town's books, payroll and every board's budget requests move through the fall town meeting season.
Dropping the roof repair article means voters will not see that item on the warrant; the funding instead stays attached to a prior appropriation for reappropriation through capital planning.
The unresolved school budget discrepancy is part of the reconciliation work that residents' questions about school funding levels depend on.

ours.headline: Entire town finance department is turning over at once; a new finance director starts October 20

watch_next: Finance Committee vote on the combined financial policies document before it goes to the Select Board
Next Finance Committee meeting, around September 11, 2025

what_happened.line: A resident asked the Finance Committee why an amount of school budget money went unspent and why the town hadn't met the school's new business manager.
Members said the school athletics revolving fund went negative and was covered using other unspent school budget money.
The town manager will merge two draft financial policy documents and bring the combined version through committee review to a vote before sending it to the Select Board.
Capital planning and debt management policy sections were tabled until the Capital Plan Committee weighs in.
The committee will skip its next scheduled meeting and reconvene around September 11.

why_it_matters: The unspent school funds and the athletics fund shortfall raised at this meeting bear on whether last year's override money and this year's added school appropriation were used as presented at town meeting.
The audit, budget, capital, and debt policies being drafted section by section will become the rules the town follows for future budgets and borrowing once the committee votes on them.
Health insurance costs and a possible full-time parks and recreation director are moving to a tri-board meeting, a step toward decisions that could affect town staffing and services.

ours.headline: FinCom reviewed draft town financial policies (audit, budget, capital, debt) line by line; no policy votes yet

watch_next: The August 26 tri-board meeting on town-school function consolidation
A future Finance Committee meeting with the finance director and/or town manager on the draft financial policy document

what_happened.line: The committee prepared questions for an August 26 tri-board meeting on merging town and school functions, including HR, IT, facilities and health insurance.
Members decided to invite the finance director and town manager to a future meeting to explain how a new draft financial policy document differs from current practice.
The committee agreed to stretch out the departmental budget submission schedule, with a written timeline to come, so meetings are not compressed as they were the prior year.
Members agreed to raise questions at their own Finance Committee meetings first so they can bring a unified position into the tri-board talks.

why_it_matters: Combining town and school HR, IT, facilities and health insurance would change how those services are staffed and paid for, a shift residents would see reflected in future budgets.
A revised budget submission calendar changes when each department's figures reach the committee, which affects how much review happens before town meeting.

ours.headline: Finance Committee reviewed draft town financial policies and readied questions for town-school department merger talks.

page.overview:
The Finance Committee is a committee of 7 members appointed for terms of 3 years, each so arranged that the terms of as nearly an equal number of members as is possible shall expire each year. The members are appointed by a committee consisting of 1 member of the Select Board chosen by the Select Board; 1 member of the School Committee chosen by the SC; and the Town Moderator.
The Finance Committee has the following duties, in accordance with the Town's Charter, Section 2-1(c):
The Finance Committee shall have the primary responsibility to report to the Town Meeting on the proposed budget of the Town Manager and all warrant articles having a fiscal impact on the Town, as more particularly detailed in the Charter, Town Bylaws, and the laws of the Commonwealth; before preparing its final recommendations, the Finance Committee shall hold 1 or more Public Hearings to permit public discussion on the subject matter of the articles contained in the warrant.
After the Town Manager has prepared the budget, the Finance Committee shall consult with the Town Manager and recommend any modifications it deems appropriate before the budget is filed with the Town Clerk.
The Finance Committee shall have all other powers conferred on finance committees by the General Laws.
For information on the Town's financial policies, please refer to the Select Board Policies and Procedures (PDF) on the Select Board Page.

page.overview:
The Agricultural Commission shall have the primary responsibility of assisting in maintaining agriculture in Lunenburg. The Commission shall administer the Right to Farm Bylaw and will hold additional responsibilities as charged by the Board of Selectmen. The Commission is a component of the state's "Sustainable Development" program, thereby helping Lunenburg become eligible for various state grant programs. The Agricultural Commission can oversee, operate or run a Farmers' Market.
The Agricultural Commission shall develop a work plan to guide its activities. Such activities may include but are not limited to, the following: encouraging the continued pursuit of agriculture in Lunenburg; promoting agricultural-based economic opportunities in Town; mediating, advocating, educating, and/or negotiating on farming issues; working for the preservation of prime agricultural lands; and pursuing all initiatives appropriate to retaining farming in Lunenburg.
"Encouraging the continued pursuit of agriculture; promoting agriculturally based economic opportunities in town; mediating, advocating, educating and/or negotiating on farming issues; working for the preservation of prime agricultural lands; and pursuing all initiatives appropriate to retaining farming in Lunenburg."
The Agricultural Commission consists of five members and two alternate members appointed by the Board of Selectmen for terms of three years each. A majority of the membership shall be substantially engaged in the pursuit of agriculture. A vacancy occurring otherwise than by expiration of a term shall be filled for the unexpired term in the same manner as the original appointment.
Anyone and everyone interested in farming, pursuing farming, or seeking to help preserve, protect, and promote Lunenburg's agricultural heritage is always welcome.

page.overview:
Welcome to the website for the Lunenburg Architectural Preservation District Commission.
The 2015 Lunenburg Town Meeting established the Architectural Preservation District ("District") Bylaw ("Bylaw") to regulate the construction, demolition, or renovation of existing "Contributing Property" structures as defined by the bylaw within an established bounded District ("District"). The Bylaw was introduced at Town Meeting along with the Village District Bylaw, which created an overlay zoning district to encourage mixed-use commercial and residential development. While the Village District Bylaw encourages the economic vitalization of downtown Lunenburg, the Architectural Preservation District Bylaw ensures that it will not come at the expense of the town's historical character and integrity.
The Bylaw also mandated the creation of Design Guidelines ("Guidelines") to assist the Architectural Preservation District Commission ("APDC") in evaluating requests for construction, renovation, and demolition of structures that are 75 years old or older within the District, as shown in the District Map (PDF).
The Select Board shall appoint a five-member APDC to oversee the APD pursuant to this bylaw. Initially, two members shall be appointed for one year, two for two years, and one for three years; each successive appointment shall be made for three years. The Select Board may also appoint up to two alternate members, initially for terms of one, two, and three years, and for three-year terms thereafter.
To the extent achievable, the APDC shall be comprised of the following persons: a member of the Lunenburg Historical Commission; a design professional; a craftsperson or building contractor familiar with historic restoration; one resident of the APD, and one resident at large. Members and alternates of the APDC shall by reason of experience and/or education have demonstrable knowledge, interest, and ability to effectively carry out the APDC's responsibilities.
To request additional information or to inquire about a non-binding Administrative Review, please email Email APDC.

what_happened.line: The Board of Assessors recommended a single, not split, tax rate for FY2026.
The board voted to reject adopting the residential exemption for the FY2026 classification.
The board also voted to reject adopting the small commercial exemption for FY2026.
The board leaned toward hiring an outside firm, rather than the citizen work group, to redo property-neighborhood boundaries after inconsistencies were flagged.
The assessor said the printed fall town meeting warrant article understated the cost of adopting COLA-linked exemption updates as zero and said it needs correcting before town meeting.

why_it_matters: A single versus split tax rate changes how the tax levy is divided between residential and commercial/industrial property, which shows up directly in individual tax bills.
Declining the residential and small commercial exemptions means the classification hearing will not shift additional tax burden between property types beyond the rate decision itself.

The COLA-linked exemption warrant article, once its cost is corrected, goes to voters at fall town meeting and is paid from the overlay account, meaning any expansion is funded by other taxpayers rather than the town budget.

what_happened.line: The board will not release the lien on a Chapter Land property until the town actually receives the owner's back-tax payment.
The town will not pursue rollback taxes on that property, instead collecting only the back taxes now owed on what has become three or four separate parcels.
The board agreed to seek a placeholder warrant article raising the veterans' property tax exemption for the November 17th special town meeting.
Review of August's already-processed excise tax abatements was pushed to the next meeting rather than taken up tonight.
The board reset its fall meeting schedule to September 23rd, October 14th, and October 28th.

why_it_matters: A property tax lien stays in force as leverage until back taxes are paid, and the town is not pursuing the larger rollback-tax penalty it could have sought on this Chapter Land property.
A veterans' exemption increase would go before voters as a warrant article at the November 17th special town meeting, and any increase is funded entirely by the town with no state reimbursement.
Routine items -- excise abatements, new-growth estimates, senior exemption applications -- remain in process rather than finalized this meeting.

page.overview:
In Massachusetts, Assessors are either appointed or elected to three-year terms. The Assessors' primary responsibility is to value all real estate and personal property subject to taxation. Assessed valuations are based on "full and fair cash value" of as of the January 1st preceding each fiscal year. Ex. For Fiscal Year 2021, the assessment date is January 1, 2020, and market sales utilized for valuation purposes are from calendar year 2019.
In order to maintain assessment at or near market value, the Assessors regularly compare property valuations with the selling prices of properties that have sold. Assessment-to-sale ration statistics are analyzed to determine the median assessment level, as well as assessment uniformity. No valuation methodology can accurately predict what a property will sell for.
Under the umbrella of Massachusetts state and local town laws, Lunenburg’s Assessing organization will work with the town operations and our citizens to meet our vision for delivering a fair and equitable taxation for our citizens. The Lunenburg Board of Assessors will evolve and administer a service of “Best Practices” methodologies consistent with our Vision. These practices will ensure equitable treatment and compassion for all our citizens.
The Board of Assessors has empowered an Assessor organization that has the capability to evaluate and assess all property at its full and fair market value. This is accomplished through a rigorous measurement of property, collection of appropriate data, analysis and maintenance of all property tax data records. Additionally, the Assessor department administers a motor vehicle excise tax, real estate and motor vehicle tax abatements, and all statutory tax exemptions as allowed by law. The Assessor Organization will work cohesively with other town departments.
The Fiscal Year 2026 tax rate is $14.39 per thousand.
Vision Statement
To provide Lunenburg with fiscal stability; by promptly, fairly and equitably determining the valuation of all real and personal property located within the geographic boundaries of Lunenburg; and execute the Assessor functions as described by Mass General Laws, the Mass Department of Revenue and the Citizens of Lunenburg.
This will be accomplished through a rigorous measurement of property, collection appropriate data, analysis and maintenance of all property tax data records. Additionally, the Assessor department will also administer a motor vehicle excise tax, real, tax abatements, and all statutory tax exemptions as allowed by law. The Assessor Organization will work cohesively with other town departments.
The Lunenburg Board of Assessors will actively reach out to the citizens of Lunenburg, to assure all members of the community are aware of all taxation practices and exemptions available. The assessors will assist with clarification these practices & exemptions, as well as guide citizens in their usage of these exemptions.
Mission Statement
Under the umbrella of Massachusetts state and local town laws; Lunenburg's Assessor organization will work with the town operations and our citizens to meet our vision for delivering a fair and equitable taxation for our citizens
The Lunenburg Board of Assessors will evolve and administer a series of “Best Practices” methodologies consistent our Vision. These practices will assure equitable treatment and compassion for all our citizens.
Board of Directors will empower an Assessor organization that will have the capability to evaluate and assess all property at its full and fair market value, for the purpose of fair and equitable taxation.
This will be accomplished through a rigorous measurement of property, collection appropriate data, analysis and maintenance of all property tax data records. Additionally, the Assessor department will also administer a motor vehicle excise tax, real, tax abatements, and all statutory tax exemptions as allowed by law. The Assessor Organization will work cohesively with other town departments.
The Lunenburg BOA activities are defined within our Town Charter.
As members of the Lunenburg Board of Assessors, (Both elected and appointed), we are in fact employees of the Town of Lunenburg, and subject to all Mass Conflict of Interest Laws and regulations: G.L c 268A.

Many of the applications for lot testing, septic system repairs/replacement, and food service can be obtained by visiting the Nashoba Associated Boards of Health website.
Visit the Department of Environmental Protection Website for information on Title 5, Hazardous waste sites, and various other topics.
The Department of Public Health website contains useful information on topics relating to public health, including information on influenza, Easter Equine Encephalitis, and West Nile Virus.
The Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources (MDAR) mission is to ensure the long-term viability of agriculture in Massachusetts. Through its four divisions - Agricultural Conservation and Technical Assistance, Agricultural Markets, Animal Health, and Crop and Pest Services - MDAR strives to support, regulate and enhance the rich diversity of the Commonwealth's agricultural community to promote economically and environmentally sound food safety and animal health measures and fulfill agriculture's role in energy conservation and production.

page.overview:
Section 1: General
The Budget Task Force shall be charged with recommending scenarios for a three to five-year sustainable fiscal plan for the Town of Lunenburg. A sustainable fiscal plan is defined as a financial forecast that uses realistic assumptions for revenue and expenditure growth that allow the Town to provide services that meet residents’ expectations and meet ongoing expenditure obligations through regularly occurring revenues. Said fiscal plan shall consider, as an example, alternative revenue sources; overrides and exclusions under proposition 2 ½; cuts in service; contracting out of services, as well as other measures. Said fiscal plan shall include both operational and capital budgets for the town. The Budget Task Force shall consult with pertinent departments as it formulates its plan.
The Budget Task Force shall present its findings and recommendations to the Select Board, Finance Committee, and School Committee no later than December 31, 2024.
Section 2: Tasks and Responsibilities
Collect data on revenue and expenditure historical trends, and project future estimates based on trends and various assumptions.
Benchmark municipal and school performance, programs, expenditures, and revenues with comparable municipalities.
Examine potential revenue sources; overrides and exclusions under Proposition 2 ½ as well as non-tax and non-override revenue sources in compliance with the Town Financial Policy including costs, feasibility, potential savings, and other impacts of potential adoption and implementation; cuts in service; contracting out of services, as well as other measures.
Evaluate strategies to properly staff municipal and school operations while managing growth of personnel costs.
Analyze capital project funding needs and impacts, including long term large capital projects.
Include both operational and capital budgets in the fiscal plan recommendations.
Assess the impact any increased taxes and fees will have on taxpayers and residents, including the tax impact of debt exclusions related to large capital projects under consideration.
Section 3: Membership and Meetings
The Select Board does hereby establish the Budget Task Force as a temporary working group consisting of seven (7) members:Select Board, 1 representative and an optional alternate appointed by it
School Committee, 1 representative and an optional alternate appointed by it
Finance Committee, 1 representative and an optional alternate appointed by it
Town Manager
School Superintendent
Town Finance Director
School Director of Administration and Finance
The Select Board shall reserve the right to continue the Budget Task Force after its task is complete in order to adjust the plan due to changing circumstances.
The Budget Task Force shall meet at a time and place mutually agreeable to its membership.
Voting Power: All duly appointed members shall have full voting power.
A quorum shall consist of four (4) members.\
The election of officers including a Chair, Vice-Chair, and Clerk shall be by a majority vote of the Budget Task Force.
The recording of minutes and votes of all meetings as prescribed by Open Meeting Law. Copies of the minutes shall be submitted to the Town Clerk as prescribed in the Town Bylaws and according to Open Meeting Law.
This charge was adopted by the Lunenburg Select Board at their June 18, 2024 meeting and may be amended at any future meeting.

On February 10, 2026 the Select Board voted to form and charge the Cable Advisory Committee in order to advise the Select Board, as Issuing Authority, relative to the license renewal with Comcast. The vote passed 4-0. Under Massachusetts regulations (207 CMR § 3.03 (3)), the Select Board may appoint a Cable Advisory Committee to advise the Issuing Authority (Select Board) through the Cable Television License Renewal process.
Charge
The Lunenburg Cable Advisory Committee shall assist the Select Board as the Issuing Authority by performing the following duties:
Select and engage with Counsel relative to the Cable Television License Renewal process
Review and evaluate the current License Agreement
Engage in the Ascertainment process, to include, but not limited to:Developing and conducting a survey or surveys;
Holding community meetings,
Meeting with Comcast representatives, together with Counsel, negotiate the License Renewal
Regularly report to the Select Board on the status of the Committee
Advise the Select Board relative to the License Renewal
Membership
The Committee shall be composed of five (5) regular members appointed by the Select Board as follows:
Two members from Public Access Cable Committee (PACC)
One member from the Select Board
Two members that are residents of Lunenburg
The Committee shall abide by the Open Meeting Law.

The goal of the Capital Planning Committee is to provide a means of planning for necessary expenditures for maintenance, equipment, and/ or improvements of the capital assets and infrastructure of the Town of Lunenburg.
The Capital Planning Committee shall research, study and advise the Selectmen and Finance Committee of the requests for short and long-range capital purchases for the Town. The Committee shall be charged with facilitating the coordination between community objectives, capital needs, and fiscal capacity. The Committee will help the Town to understand the tax impact of the capital expenditures and consider the relative need, timing, and cost of each capital expenditure. The Committee shall consider all written requests and make recommendations. The Committee shall provide a written report to assist the Selectmen and Finance Committee in keeping the community informed about the Town's future anticipated needs and projects that will be voted on at the Annual Town Meeting.
The Capital Planning Committee receives its authorization from Article 27 of the Town's Bylaws which states, "There shall be a Capital Planning Committee. That Committee shall consist of five members to be appointed as follows: One member each designated by the Financial Committee, the Select Board, the School Committee, and the Planning Board, and a fifth member chosen at large by the Town Moderator. Each member shall be appointed for a term of three years, said terms staggered so that nearly an equal number of members shall be appointed each year. The Capital Planning Committee shall establish and update a comprehensive capital plan.
The committee shall at least annually provide its materials to the Chief Administrative and Financial Officer so that the Chief Administrative and Financial Officer will meet the obligations of the Office set forth in Section 6-6 (sic) of the Lunenburg Town Charter. The Capital Planning Committee shall be responsible for providing a complete inventory of town property, real and personal, including school property, in conjunction with the Chief Administrative and Financial Officer. (ATM 5/05/07, Art.21)

The Cemetery Commission is an elected three-member Commission with terms of three years each. The board of cemetery commissioners have the responsibility to make regulations governing the care, superintendence, and management of all public burial grounds in Lunenburg and to lay out existing public burial grounds and may lot out in lots or other suitable subdivision with proper paths, lanes, and ways appropriate for burial use any other land acquired by the town for burial purposes. The day-to-day care and maintenance of the cemeteries shall be under the supervision of the Town Manager, which has been delegated to the DPW Director as the Cemetery is a division under the Department of Public Works.
Lunenburg has two major cemeteries:
North Cemetery is located on Holman Street at the corner of Highland Street
South Cemetery is located on Page Street off Lancaster Avenue

page.overview:
At least once every ten years a special committee consisting of nine members shall be established for the purpose of reviewing the Town Charter and making a report, with recommendations, to the Town Meeting concerning proposed amendments which said committee may determine to be necessary or desirable. The committee shall consist of nine members who shall be chosen as follows: the Select Board, the Finance Committee and the School Committee shall each designate two persons, the Planning Board shall designate one person and two persons shall be appointed by the Town Moderator.
Persons appointed by the agencies may, but need not be members of the agency by which they are designated. The committee shall organize forthwith following the final adjournment of the Annual Town Meeting.
Members and Contact Information are to be determined.

The storm water utility warrant article, as submitted for an upcoming town meeting

what_happened.line: The commission approved the Lake Shirley boat ramp rebuild at Shady Point, granting waivers to work inside the normal 30-foot no-disturb and 50-foot no-build wetland buffers.
Four other wetland hearings, including a new house and driveway at 404 Page Street, were continued to October 7 rather than decided.
The commission approved three routine RDAs with standard conditions: a DPW cemetery expansion, a septic force main repair, and a shed/sand permit.
A non-binding warrant article was finalized asking whether storm water funding should move out of the operating budget into a dedicated storm water utility.
A vote on replacing flooring at the town-owned Hollis Road residence was deferred pending clarification of a vendor's deposit request.

why_it_matters: The boat ramp decision sets a precedent for allowing construction inside protected wetland buffers along Lake Shirley when a project shows a public benefit.

The storm water warrant article, if it reaches town meeting, would ask voters to decide whether storm water work gets its own dedicated funding stream instead of competing inside the general operating budget.
Residents near 404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, and 141 Pleasant Street will have another chance to be heard before any of those projects are decided.

ours.headline: Conservation Commission approved the Lake Shirley boat ramp rebuild with wetland buffer waivers.

watch_next: September 16, 2026 continued hearings: 701 Reservoir Road, 108 Sunny Hill Road, 157 Goodridge Street
Storm water utility warrant article, still in drafting

what_happened.line: The Commission voted 5-0 to accept a redesigned ADA trail route at Cowry Nature Center that avoids direct wetland alteration.
Three other wetlands hearings -- a boat ramp, a driveway crossing, and an irrigation pond -- were continued to September 16 after documents arrived late.
The Commission voted 5-0 to approve draft bylaw amendments to move toward town meeting.
A storm water committee is drafting a warrant article for a storm water utility because the operating budget cannot fund the DPW's required catch-basin and culvert cleaning.
The Commission approved an amount as heard purchase for smoke and CO2 detectors at its Hollis Road property.

why_it_matters: The ADA trail redesign changes how a town-funded accessibility project reaches Cowry Nature Center and keeps it clear of wetland permitting delays.
The bylaw amendments the Commission approved will come before town meeting, where residents get a vote.
A storm water utility warrant article, if it advances, could mean a new fee tied to the town's stormwater permit obligations.

ours.headline: Commission voted to redesign the Cowry Nature Center ADA trail route to avoid direct wetland alteration.

page.overview:
The Conservation Commission is a seven-member commission, the members of which are appointed to staggered three-year terms by the Select Board. The Conservation Commission enforces the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act and the Lunenburg Wetlands Protection By-law. The Commission also has care and custody of over 24 publicly accessible properties that are permanently protected for conservation and passive recreation.

what_happened.line: Council on Aging agreed to seek capital-plan funding for a parking lot redesign at the senior center.
Board decided to write its own entry for the town report, separate from the director's operational report.
Board turned down joining a multi-town "friendly neighbors" program and will instead expand its own friendly visitors program.
Director will send the board the FY26 year-end financial report after confusion over the current gift fund balance.
Chair will ask whether Lunenburg can be added to the ambulance catchment area of a new UMass emergency facility in Groton.

why_it_matters: A capital-plan request puts the senior center parking lot and ADA access into the town's capital budget process, where it will compete with other town projects for funding.
The gift fund balance confusion and the push for regular financial reports touch how residents can track money donated to the Council on Aging.
Whether Lunenburg joins the new Groton facility's EMS catchment area could affect ambulance response for seniors and others in town.

page.overview:
The Lunenburg Cultural Council is responsible for disbursing funds received from the Massachusetts Cultural Council for local cultural and artistic activities.
The mission of the Lunenburg Cultural Council is to nurture and promote a diverse range of artistic and cultural programs for the benefit of Lunenburg and surrounding communities.
We accomplish this through the annual allocation of state grants for local projects and by producing cultural events using locally-raised funds.
The Council reviews proposals and grants funds to local applicants for a variety of projects that benefit Lunenburg citizens. Local Cultural Councils support community-based projects in the arts, sciences, and humanities every year. The state legislature provides an annual appropriation to the Massachusetts Cultural Council, a state agency, which then allocates funds to each community.
The Lunenburg Cultural Council recognizes that the arts, humanities, and interpretive sciences form an important part of Lunenburg's history, identity, and vision. We are committed to nurturing our artistic community through supporting events that are accessible, collaborative, and fun for Lunenburg residents and visitors of all ages.

page.overview:
Section 1: General
The Lunenburg Economic Development Committee is being formed by the Planning Board in order to better assist, counsel, and advise the residents of Lunenburg, the Planning Board, other Town Boards and Departments, and Lunenburg businesses on ways to promote the local economy.
Section 2: Functions
Mission: The Lunenburg Economic Development Committee is committed to promoting business development that will enhance the character, culture, and commerce in Lunenburg. The Committee shall investigate current economic conditions to provide advice to Town Departments on economic development policy; meet and work with current Lunenburg businesses and prospective businesses; coordinate its activities with the appropriate Town Boards and Commissions; and work cooperatively with businesses and state agencies to retain, develop and promote businesses in Lunenburg.
Section 3: Membership & Meetings
The Committee shall be composed of five regular members serving three-year terms appointed by the Planning Board as follows: One member recommended by the Agricultural Commission that owns a business in Lunenburg and shall initially be appointed for a three-year term; One member recommended by the Open Space Committee and shall initially be appointed for a three-year term; One member recommended by the Conservation Commission and shall initially be appointed for a two-year term; Two members that are residents of Lunenburg, one shall initially be appointed for a two-year term and one shall initially be appointed for a one year term. In addition to the regular members, there will be four ex-officio members as follows: One member of the Select Board chosen annually by the Select Board; One member of the Planning Board chosen annually by the Planning Board; The Director of Planning and Economic Development; and A Lunenburg Business Owner.
After the initial term, all members shall serve a three-year term.
Voting Power: All duly appointed members shall have full voting power; ex-officio members shall not have the power to vote.
Resignation: Members of the Committee shall notify the Chairman of the Committee and the Planning Board of their resignation.
Vacancies: Any vacancies shall be filled in the same manner as the original appointment.
The election of officers including at least a Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Clerk and shall be elected annually by a majority vote of the Committee.
A quorum shall consist of three members.
The Committee shall keep a recording of minutes and votes of all meetings as prescribed by the Open Meeting Law. This charge may be amended at any time.
New way to complete your Business Identity Certificate:
For people planning on opening a new business in Lunenburg, the Town Clerk’s NEW Business Identity Certificate (BIC) is now available to be completed as part of Building Department’s Form of Intent found here: Business Identity Certificate (BIC) You will still need to print out the BIC and hand-deliver to the Town Clerk’s office, but now the form can be completed and generated online.
New Business Ribbon Cutting Ceremony:
On Thursday August 6, the Town of Lunenburg's Economic Development Committee proudly hosted its first ribbon cutting ceremony, celebrating the continued growth of Diligent Digital Marketing Corp. as the company expands into a larger office in Lunenburg. The event welcomed the business to its new space at 1 Main Street and marked the beginning of a new tradition recognizing business investment and success in our community.
Founded by Chris Kostecki, Diligent Digital Marketing Corp. has grown from a sole proprietorship into a full-service digital marketing consulting firm.
Chris was joined by members of his family, Economic Development Committee Members Joeci Gilchrest and Cathy Clark, State Representative Mike Kushmerek, State Representative Margaret Scarsdale, Beth Walsh, Constituent Services Director for State Senator John Cronin, Roy Nascimento, President & CEO of the North Central Massachusetts Chamber of Commerce, Chamber Staff and Members, Select Board members Renee Emkey, Brian Lehtinen, and Glenn McLeod, and Town Manager Jennifer Warren-Dyment.
Congratulations to Chris and the entire Diligent team on this exciting milestone. We wish you continued success and are proud that your business continues to grow right here in Lunenburg.

page.overview:
Section 1: General
The Lunenburg Green Communities Committee will work with the Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources to learn of grant opportunities for energy conservation and renewable energy generation and will apply for appropriate grants. The Committee will ensure the Town retains its status as a designated Green Community.
Section 2: Functions
Mission: The Lunenburg Green Communities Committee will focus on improving and promoting energy efficiency in town and school facilities, infrastructure, and vehicles. The Committee will help raise awareness, educate, advise, and motivate the Town of Lunenburg residents and businesses to reduce waste, reduce energy use, conserve resources, reduce emissions/carbon footprint, and embrace clean and renewable energy options.
Responsibilities
Identify and develop grant submissions for Green Communities Competitive Grant annually that corresponds with the mission of this committee and is consistent with the Town's goals;
Develop action steps to ensure Lunenburg remains designated as a Department of Energy Resources Green Community;
Facilitate town participation in DOER programs, grants, and incentives;
Serve as an information resource for town residents and business owners on the benefits of energy and resource conservation;
Increase constituents' awareness of and promote resource conservation methods, energy efficiency programs, utility rebates, and state/federal programs to promote energy efficiency, waste reduction, recycling, and overall enhancements to long-term sustainability and resilience in response to environmental, resource, and energy challenges;
Report at least once annually on its activities to the Select Board.
Section 3: Membership & Meetings
The Committee shall be composed of 5 regular members serving three-year terms appointed by the Select Board and two associate members. Two members shall initially be appointed to a three-year term, two members shall initially be appointed to a two-year term, and one member shall initially be appointed to a one-year term. After the initial term, all regular members shall serve a three-year term. The associate members shall be appointed to a three-year term.
In addition to the regular members, the Committee shall consult with the Town Manager, the town departments that oversee the facilities and energy accounts, the School Superintendent, and the School Facilities Director that oversees the school facilities and school energy accounts in order to ascertain future energy projects, areas where energy savings are needed, and replacement schedule for vehicles.
Voting Power: All duly appointed regular members shall have full voting power.
Resignation: Members of the Committee shall notify the Chairman of the Committee, the Town Manager, and the Select Board of their resignation.
Vacancies: Any vacancies shall be filled in the same manner as the original appointment.
Representations: Members shall get the approval of the Committee prior to making statements, presentations, or joining activities on behalf of the Committee.
The election of officers including at least a Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Clerk and shall be elected annually by a majority vote of the Committee.
A quorum shall consist of three members.
The recording of minutes and votes of all meetings shall be conducted as prescribed by the Open Meeting Law. Copies of the minutes shall be submitted to the Town Clerk as prescribed in the Town Bylaw and according to Open Meeting Law.
The Committee shall comply with all state laws and local bylaws.
This charge was adopted by the Select Board at their June 1, 2021 meeting and may be amended at any future meeting.

The Historical Commission shall act for the preservation, protection, and development of the historical or archeological assets of the Town. The commission shall conduct research for places of historic or archeological value, shall seek to coordinate the activities of unofficial bodies organized for similar purposes, and may advertise, prepare, print, and distribute materials that it deems necessary for its work. It shall make recommendations to the Select Board that any place be certified as a historical landmark. The commission may hold hearings and may enter into contracts with individuals, organizations, and institutions for services furthering their objectives.
The commission may acquire in the name of the Town by gift, purchase, grant, bequest, devise, lease, or otherwise, the fee or lesser interest in real or personal property of significant historical value and may manage the same. The commission shall file an annual report which shall be included in the Annual Town Report.
The Historical Commission shall be composed of five (5) members appointed by the Select Board for terms of three years each with said terms staggered so that as nearly an equal number of members shall be appointed each year.

page.overview:
Lunenburg Public Library welcomes all and serves residents of the Lunenburg area as a hub for the community, enriching our lives through its collections, programs, services, facility, and people.
Please visit the Lunenburg Public Library Website for library resources, latest news, and events.
Powers and Duties - The Board of Trustees shall act as an agent of the public trust governing the library. The library shall create the general operating and administrative policies relating to budget, personnel, and contracts as specified by state law and local ordinances. All funds raised or appropriated by the town for the support and maintenance of the library shall be expended under the direction of the board. All funds that the town may receive by gift, bequest, or otherwise for library purposes shall be administered under the direction of the board in accordance with the terms of such gift, bequest, or otherwise. The board shall hire and manage the library director. The responsibilities and governance of the board shall cover the following specific areas: (i) legal; (ii) policy making; (iii) financial governance; and (iv) strategic planning. The board shall, in all matters of general municipal policy and procedure, be subject to policy directives designed to achieve uniformity and better administrative control as may from time to time be established by the town manager. The library director shall exercise professional judgment under the direction and review of the board to implement the strategic objectives and policies set by the board. The library director shall be responsible for the day-to-day administration of the library, including management of personnel, collection development, budget, physical plant, and programmatic functions, subject to policy directives established by the board. The library director shall work in conjunction with the board on strategic planning and library policies.
The Library Director shall prepare an annual budget for approval by the board. The library director shall hire library employees, fix their salaries, define their duties, make rules concerning their tenure of office and discharge them in accordance with and within the limits established by the town personnel by-laws, policies, procedures, and practices and any applicable collective bargaining agreement, in accordance with municipal policies. The board shall make all reasonable rules and regulations for the operation and management of the library system and for the conduct of its own business and affairs as may be deemed necessary. The board shall have all of the other powers and duties that are given to library trustees by general law, this charter, by-law, or other vote of the town meeting.
Composition, Term of Office - There shall be a board of trustees of the public library consisting of 7 members, elected for terms of 3 years each, so arranged that the terms of as nearly an equal number of members as is possible shall expire each year.

page.overview:
The year 2028 will mark the 300th Anniversary of the incorporation of the Town of Lunenburg. In order to recognize and celebrate Lunenburg's Tricentennial, the residents of Lunenburg, by Town Meeting vote of May 7, 2022, authorized and established a steering committee, subsequently designated the "Lunenburg 300th Anniversary Committee," and hereinafter referred to as "the Committee."
The Committee shall be comprised of no greater than 11 members, each of whom shall be appointed by the Select Board for a term to begin on the date of appointment and terminate when, as determined by a vote of the Select Board, the Committee has discharged all of its defined functions and is dissolved. As a body, the Committee shall:
Develop a celebratory plan including a timeline, proposed events, publicity plan, volunteer roster, funding requirements, and funding sources.
Coordinate with other entities and officials within the Town government, including the police chief, fire chief, DPW director, historical commission, and superintendent of schools, in order to facilitate safety and maximize resident participation.
Solicit, evaluate, and generate recommendations as to how the Town should manage the commemoration of its tricentennial, and the celebration of its rich history.
Oversee subcommittees established for specified purposes, and supervise and assist these subcommittees in their functions.
Recruit, organize, task, and oversee volunteers from among the townspeople in furtherance of the overall celebration and the execution of specific functions of the Committee and/or its subcommittees.
Plan, coordinate, manage, sponsored, and implement commemorative events including, but not limited to, recreational and educational activities and social/cultural gatherings intended to enhance the townspeople's awareness and appreciation for the history of the Town and the contributions that its residents have made locally and nationally to various fields of human endeavor including, for example, architecture, arts, civil rights, government, engineering, environmental protection, industry, invention, law, literature, medicine, the military, politics, public policy, public safety, and science.
Encourage through effective communication and outreach maximum inclusion, attendance, and participation by the townspeople in events and celebrations.
Partner with local businesses and community organizations to develop events that appeal to all ages and encourage maximum participation by town residents.

what_happened.line: The committee voted that the Ritter Building's current square footage cannot fit all town hall functions.
A guest presenter outlined using the TC Pasios site for senior housing, a community center, and a town green.
Committee agreed to have a feasibility study scope three versions of the TC Pasios plan before the next meeting.
Committee agreed to draft a joint square-footage and cost document, comparing renovation to a new addition, for the Select Board.
Failing boilers at TC Pasios were discussed as threatening its teen center and food pantry tenants once it gets cold, with no vote taken.

why_it_matters: The vote that the Ritter Building is too small moves the committee toward proposing an addition, a project that would eventually need Select Board and town meeting approval.
The TC Pasios feasibility study could determine whether that site becomes senior housing, a community center, a town green, or some combination -- a choice residents may later vote to fund.
Unrepaired boilers at TC Pasios put the building's teen center and food pantry programs at risk of losing usable space this winter.

page.overview:
The Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee (formerly the TC Passios Building Design Committee) will continue to work with any contracted architectural and engineering firms, as they become available, to review space needs for town offices, school uses and community space at the building and/or land known as the TC Passios.
Additionally, the committee will work to prioritize and/or rank the existing space usage requests and explore a variety of design permutations at different estimated budget tiers that would meet the needs of the Town according to those priorities. The committee may analyze, discuss and investigate other Town-owned buildings and properties in their recommendations as they deem necessary to fulfill this charge.
This Committee will prepare viable, cost-effective solutions for the Select Board that conform to all the Town's existing financial and fiscal policies and take into consideration any/all large-scale capital expenditures projected for the next 10 years. This charge was amended by the Select Board at their January 4, 2022 meeting and may be amended at any future meeting. At the July 15, 2025 meeting of the Select Board, it was voted to add a member from the Architectural Preservation District Commission to the composition of the LMBDC and reduced the quorum to four.
